item.title: Upcoming news
Apple's First Earnings Report Under New CEO Shows Strong Revenue but Missed Targets in China and iPad
item.description: Apple reported strong financial results for its third quarter, with revenue reaching $114.5 billion, surpassing Wall Street estimates of $113.46 billion. Earnings per share came in at $2.10, exceeding analysts' expectations of $2. The company's iPhone segment generated $57.58 billion in revenue, slightly above estimates of $56.48 billion. However, China revenue of $17.54 billion fell short of the $18.75 billion analysts had predicted, and iPad sales at $6.23 billion missed the $6.83 billion estimate. Mac sales, at $10.79 billion, outperformed estimates by over $1 billion. Apple's Services business reported $31.57 billion, aligning closely with forecasts. CFO Kevan Parekh explained that gross margins were boosted by tariff refunds, and without these refunds, margins would have decreased due to higher memory costs. The company's new CEO, John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook on September 1, delivered his first earnings report on Monday. Ternus highlighted iPhone and Mac performance wh

item.title: AI Agent Successfully Performs Brain Injection on Live Mouse in Biotech Experiment
item.description: A biotech startup, Exin Therapeutics, led by CEO Gabriel Ocana Santero, recently conducted an experiment where an AI agent successfully performed a brain injection procedure on a live mouse. The AI agent, using a custom-built surgical setup, selected a gene therapy treatment from 19 options, determined the injection coordinates, and controlled robotic arms and an injector needle to deliver the compound. The experiment aimed to test a gene therapy for reducing seizures in a mouse with epilepsy. The team initially used Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 model, which refused to guide the needle into the mouse's brain, citing potential risks. They switched to Claude Sonnet 5, which agreed to proceed. Despite technical glitches, including a coordinate system error that required a separate AI agent to make code changes, the procedure was completed successfully. The AI agent was designed with safeguards, including human approval for injection plans and an emergency stop button. The experiment took s

item.title: Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered conversation tools for note-taking and sound detection
item.description: Apple has begun beta testing its new 'Audio Intelligence' technology for the Apple Watch Series 12, which includes four AI-powered features designed to enhance user experience through sound recognition and conversation management. The technology, first announced at Apple's September Surprise and Shine event, is now available in the iOS 27.3 beta update for developers. The four features include sound detection for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, song recognition via Shazam, Live Rewind for reviewing recent conversations, and Siri Recaps for summarizing discussions. The sound detection feature helps users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells through the watch, while song recognition identifies music playing in the background. Live Rewind allows users to review the last 15 seconds of conversation by double-pressing the digital crown, with the option to save the text snippet to the Siri app. Siri Recaps goes further by summarizing conversations into key points withou

item.title: Cyberattacks Target Supermarket Refrigeration Systems Across Multiple European Countries
item.description: A series of cyberattacks have targeted refrigeration systems in supermarkets across several European countries, including Ireland, Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, and Estonia. The incidents, occurring less than a month after a similar attack affected hundreds of supermarkets in France, have caused temperatures in fridges and freezers to rise sharply, leading to spoiled food and significant financial losses. In Ireland, SuperValu, the country's third-largest supermarket chain, reported that 13 of its 223 stores were affected by a cyber incident involving a specific refrigerator model, resulting in the removal of chilled and frozen products from sale. Swedish stores operated by ICA and Co-op experienced similar issues, with freezer temperatures reaching 50°C overnight. Belgian and Luxembourgish stores under Ahold Delhaize also faced disruptions, with Carrefour reporting 15 out of 700 stores in Belgium affected and five Spar stores under Colruyt Group impacted. item.title: Mutiara Ayu Puspitasari Advances to Korea Open Main Draw After Dominant Qualifying Win
item.description:
Indonesian women's singles badminton player Mutiara Ayu Puspitasari has qualified for the main draw of the 2026 Korea Open after defeating Ukraine's Yevheniia Kantemyr in straight games on Tuesday, November 3, in Yeosu, South Korea. Mutiara secured a convincing 21-5, 21-6 victory in the final qualifying round, comfortably controlling the match despite experiencing some early difficulties.
Although the score suggested a one-sided contest, Mutiara admitted that adapting to the court conditions initially proved challenging. She explained that the playing surface felt noticeably different from the one used during her previous practice session, making it difficult to establish her rhythm at the beginning of the match.
She also acknowledged that Kantemyr's experience competing at this level briefly complicated her efforts to determine the right playing strategy. However, once she adjusted to the conditions and identified an effective approach, Mutiara was able to dictate the pace and contr

item.title: Marine Biomedical secures FDA approval for pearl shell-based bone graft, expanding Orthocell's US market access
item.description: Marine Biomedical, a strategic partner of Orthocell, has received US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 510(k) clearance for PearlBone, a bone graft substitute made from pearl shell sourced sustainably from Western Australia's Kimberley region. The FDA clearance allows PearlBone to be marketed in the United States for its intended indications, marking a significant milestone for both companies as they aim to enter one of the world's largest medical device markets. Orthocell, an Australian biotech company listed on the ASX (ASX:OCC), finalized a strategic investment in Marine Biomedical in January 2026, increasing its equity stake to 12% through a $1.05 million investment. This investment also secured Orthocell a first right of refusal over global distribution rights for PearlBone and future bone repair and regeneration products. PearlBone leverages the natural properties of nacre, the biomineralized structure of pearl shell, to support bone repair and regeneration. The product is manuf

item.title: Ellen DeGeneres Honors Late Executive Producer Matthew Wright as 'The Glue' of Her Show Family
item.description: Ellen DeGeneres expressed deep sorrow following the death of Matthew Wright, a former executive producer of The Ellen DeGeneres Show, who passed away on October 30, 2026, in Los Angeles at the age of 52. In an emotional social media post, the 68-year-old television personality shared heartfelt memories of Wright, describing him as "an amazing guy" who was "funny" and "made me laugh" with his spontaneous gestures. She emphasized his kindness and intelligence, stating that "everyone loved him" and that his passing was "shocking." Wright had served as executive producer for 16 years, from the show's inception until its conclusion in 2022, playing a pivotal role in shaping the daytime program. DeGeneres revealed that she and Wright had been planning a new collaboration before his death, which made the loss even more poignant. In her post, she reflected on Wright's significance to the show's team, calling him "the glue to our entire family at the Ellen Show." Wright had previously shared hi

item.title: Russia Expands Its Influence in Africa but Remains Far Behind China Economically
item.description:
Russia has increased its influence across Africa over the past decade, but its economic presence remains significantly smaller than China's, according to an analysis published by bne IntelliNews on November 2, 2026. Based on the University of Denver's Foreign Bilateral Influence Capacity index, Russia's share of foreign influence in Africa rose from 2.2% in 2015 to 2.8% in 2024, moving it from 12th to ninth place among the continent's international partners. China leads with 11%, followed by France and the United States at 7% each.
Russia's growing influence is largely based on military cooperation, food exports, and nuclear energy projects rather than trade and investment. Bilateral trade with African countries reached $30.4 billion in 2025, more than double the 2015 figure. However, this represents only around 1.5% of Africa's foreign trade. China's merchandise trade with the continent reached a record $348 billion in 2025, more than 12 times Russia's total.

item.title: Bears' Dominant Performance Against Seahawks Highlights NFC North Leadership
item.description: The Chicago Bears secured a decisive 34-17 victory over the Seattle Seahawks on Monday Night Football, demonstrating their status as the most complete team in the NFC North division. Led by quarterback Caleb Williams and head coach Ben Johnson, the Bears' offense and defense combined for a dominant performance. Williams completed 237 passing yards, including a touchdown to Luther Burden III, and became the first quarterback to surpass 200 passing yards against the Seahawks' top-ranked defense in yards allowed per game. The Bears' ground game, spearheaded by D'Andre Swift's three touchdowns, was a key factor, supported by a disciplined offensive line. On defense, All-Pro Jeffery Simmons made an immediate impact in his first game with the Bears, recording six combined tackles, a sack, and two tackles for loss. item.title: Sudan Accuses Ethiopia of Allowing RSF Drone Attacks From Its Territory
item.description:
Sudan's government has accused Ethiopia of allowing the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) to launch drone attacks against civilian infrastructure from Ethiopian territory. Khartoum has filed formal complaints with the United Nations Security Council and the African Union's Peace and Security Council, seeking international accountability.
The Sudanese Foreign Ministry said it submitted documents alleging that the RSF used missile-equipped drones launched from Ethiopia to strike civilian sites and critical facilities across Sudan. According to the ministry, the attacks caused civilian casualties and disrupted essential services. It described the alleged operations as hostile acts and violations of international law, citing Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, which prohibits the use of force against another state's territorial integrity or political independence. Ethiopia had not immediately responded to the accusations.

item.title: MAGA Conservatives Adopt Star Wars Memes to Promote Far-Right Ideology
item.description: The article discusses how Trump supporters and MAGA conservatives are using Star Wars memes, particularly focusing on Anakin Skywalker's transformation into Darth Vader, to promote far-right political messaging ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The content describes how these memes depict Anakin as a 'disenfranchised chud' who becomes radicalized against a 'corrupt political order,' mirroring conservative grievances about issues like immigration, DEI (Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion), and perceived Democratic overreach. The article notes that figures like Elon Musk have shared AI-generated images of Anakin on a throne with his family, declaring 'This is what they stole from us,' while right-wing influencers claim these memes represent a 'culturally significant' anti-progressive movement. item.title: Learjet Crash Investigation Points to Ice and Weather as Key Factors
item.description: A Learjet traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas crashed on Sunday afternoon near Palm Beach, Florida, resulting in nine fatalities. The aircraft, a Bombardier-made two-engine jet, encountered a thunderstorm cell at 35,000 feet around 12:48 p.m., with the co-pilot reporting light, clear ice and moderate turbulence to air traffic control. Federal officials have stated that ice and weather conditions were 'certainly a factor' in the crash, though the investigation is ongoing and may take months to conclude. The crash left a crater resembling a bomb blast, and audio recordings of the final moments between the co-pilot and air traffic control have circulated online, adding to the urgency of understanding what transpired. The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation, with officials cautioning that it is too early to determine the exact cause. The incident has raised questions about aviation safety in adverse weather conditions, particularly regarding ice accum

item.title: White Dwarf's Debris Rings Offer Clues to Solar System's Future
item.description: Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have identified a white dwarf star, J1328−1450, located approximately 1,600 light-years from Earth, surrounded by two distinct rings of gas and dust. These debris rings, observed using the Very Large Telescope, are believed to be remnants of a planetary system that once orbited the star. As the star evolved from a red giant phase into a white dwarf, it likely destroyed some of its planets, leaving behind rocky bodies exposed to extreme conditions. The resulting debris formed the observed rings, which may provide insight into the future of our own solar system. In about 5 billion years, the Sun will exhaust its fuel, expand into a red giant, and potentially engulf nearby planets before shedding its outer layers to become a white dwarf. Any surviving rocky bodies could then break apart, forming a debris disk similar to the one observed around J1328−1450. item.title: 1970s America: Industrial Pollution and Daily Life Captured in Rare Color Photographs
item.description: The 1970s in America were marked by a complex interplay between industrial growth and everyday life, as revealed through a collection of color photographs commissioned by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under the Documerica project. These images document the stark reality of pollution in residential areas, with industrial smokestacks towering over neighborhoods, chemical plants lining waterways, and communities exposed to hazardous substances like arsenic and lead. In Ruston, Washington, children played in yards while a nearby smelter released toxic residue, and in Birmingham, Alabama, homes stood adjacent to a U.S. Steel plant, with industrial smog enveloping the area. The photographs also capture moments of ordinary life, such as weddings, neighborhood gatherings, and personal celebrations, offering a nuanced view of the era. item.title: MAGA lawmaker blocks Bloomberg access following campaign scandal coverage
item.description: U.S. Representative Mike Lawler (R-NY) participated in a press conference with House Problem Solvers Caucus members on gerrymandering reform on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on September 16, 2026, as captured by Reuters photographer Aaron Schwartz. According to a report by Matthew Chapman, a journalist who attended Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and resides in San Marcos, Texas, a MAGA-affiliated lawmaker has revoked Bloomberg's access after the news organization reported on a campaign scandal. Chapman, who previously wrote for Shareblue and AlterNet specializing in election and policy coverage, provided this information in his article published on November 2, 2026, at 9:56 PM ET. item.title: Ann Rutherford: Hollywood's 1930s Starlet in Rare Vintage Portraits
item.description: Therese Ann Rutherford (November 2, 1917 – June 11, 2012), a Canadian-born American actress, rose to prominence during the 1930s through her roles in family films and classic cinema. Beginning her career as a teenager by falsifying an acting resume to secure a radio role at KFAC in Los Angeles, Rutherford quickly transitioned to film. Her early on-screen debut came in the 1934 film 'Student Tour,' followed by leading roles at Republic Pictures, where she became a staple in B-Westerns alongside stars like John Wayne and Gene Autry. In 1937, Rutherford landed a pivotal role as Polly Benedict in the 'Andy Hardy' series, playing the dependable girlfriend of Andy Hardy (Mickey Rooney), which cemented her status as a household name representing the idealized American teenager. Her career reached a new height when she secured the role of Carreen O'Hara in 'Gone with the Wind' (1939) after personally lobbying producer David O. Selznick. item.title: Justice Department Seeks to Prevent Jack Smith's Deposition in Trump's BBC Defamation Case
item.description:
The U.S. Department of Justice has moved to prevent former special counsel Jack Smith from being deposed in President Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), according to a report by The Guardian.
The Justice Department sent a letter to Smith's attorneys on Monday, November 2, informing them that the agency would not authorize his testimony in the case. A judge had previously ordered Smith to participate in a deposition, potentially as early as December 11.
Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in 2025, alleging that the broadcaster deceptively edited footage of his speech at the Ellipse in Washington, D.C., on January 6, 2021. According to Trump's complaint, the editing made it appear that he had encouraged supporters to attack the U.S. Capitol. The lawsuit seeks $10 billion in damages.

item.title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump's Request to Set Aside 20,000 California Ballots
item.description:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration's emergency request to intervene in a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to set aside 20,000 ballots in California that officials flagged as potentially cast by noncitizens.
The Justice Department had argued that the ballots should be withheld until the citizenship of the voters could be verified. However, multiple lower courts had already rejected efforts to remove the ballots from the electoral process, finding insufficient grounds to justify such action. During court arguments, the DOJ also acknowledged that its list of potentially ineligible voters could contain significant errors.
The Supreme Court's decision prompted an angry reaction from several prominent supporters of President Donald Trump and conservative commentators on social media platform X. Far-right lawyer Mike Davis described the justices as cowards, while Chaya Raichik, who operates the LibsOfTikTok account, criticized the decision as unbelievable.

item.title: Hackers Send Fake Nuclear Attack Alerts to Ukraine and Russia
item.description: On November 1-2, 2026, Ukraine's Air Alert app and Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry app were both hacked, sending users false warnings about nuclear attacks, chemical threats, and street fighting in Kyiv. The first breach occurred on Sunday evening, November 1, when Ukraine's Air Alert app displayed fake alerts in Russian, including a message stating, 'Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine now. Don't worry, Oreshnik is on its way.' The app became temporarily unavailable, and Ukraine's Air Force dismissed the warnings as 'hostile interference,' urging users not to follow third-party links or spread unverified information. Hours later, Russian users received fake alerts on the Emergency Situations Ministry app, claiming nuclear warheads had been launched toward every region of Russia. The alerts falsely attributed the attack to Ukrainian-made P1-SUN drones, instructing users to stockpile food and seek shelter. Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry reported a 'massive at

item.title: Dan Rather Warns Trump's Behavior Could Hurt Republicans in the Midterm Elections
item.description:
Veteran journalist Dan Rather has warned that President Donald Trump's increasingly unpredictable behavior could become a political liability for Republicans ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. In a new essay published on his Substack newsletter, Ready, Rather argued that recent public appearances by Trump suggest growing political concerns within the Republican Party as Democrats make gains in several key Senate races.
Rather highlighted Trump's Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida, where the president spoke to reporters about the wealthy friends attending the event. He also criticized Trump's appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., on Monday, describing the event as an opportunity for Trump to promote his personal vision of the nation's capital rather than make a political case for Republican candidates.

item.title: Trump Administration Conducts Strike Against Iranian Missile Launcher Ahead of Midterm Elections
item.description:
The Trump administration has drawn criticism after a U.S. military strike destroyed an Iranian surface-to-air missile launcher on Qeshm Island, raising concerns about a potential escalation of the conflict between the United States and Iran just before the 2026 midterm elections.
According to Barak Ravid, global affairs correspondent for Axios, a U.S. fighter jet carried out the operation on Monday night. Citing a senior U.S. official, Ravid reported that the strike was conducted in self-defense after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched an anti-aircraft missile from the launcher. The American aircraft subsequently destroyed the weapons system.
The reported operation has prompted concerns about the direction of the conflict, particularly as the Trump administration faces mounting political pressure ahead of the midterm elections. item.title: Right-Wing Commentators Promote Doomsday Preparations Amid Republican Midterm Election Concerns
item.description:
Right-wing commentators and political figures are encouraging Americans to prepare for a potential global catastrophe, prompting speculation and alarm as Republicans face the possibility of significant losses in the 2026 midterm elections. According to The Bulwark's Will Sommer, the messaging has intensified since late October, with several prominent conservative personalities warning their audiences about unspecified threats.
The trend gained momentum after the United Kingdom advised households to maintain emergency supplies. Some right-wing social media accounts portrayed the guidance, alongside similar recommendations previously issued in Europe, as evidence of an impending international crisis. Attention increased further following a Fox News report about the Pentagon's FORTRESS initiative, which is designed to enable domestic military bases to operate independently for up to 90 days.

item.title: Trump's Midterm Question Responses Draw Criticism from Analyst
item.description: The article discusses an incident involving former U.S. President Donald Trump during a press briefing at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on October 29, 2026. During the event, Trump was questioned about midterm election strategies but appeared to struggle with the questions, leading to criticism from analysts. The headline 'Analyst floored as 'impressively disconnected' Trump fumbles midterm questions: 'Insane'' suggests that Trump's performance was notably disjointed and unprepared. The article, written by Robert Davis, an award-winning journalist and senior editor at RawStory, highlights the analyst's reaction to Trump's apparent lack of coherence during the questioning. The piece includes a photo caption from Reuters showing Trump speaking to reporters before boarding Air Force One for travel to South Carolina. item.title: Student protests erupt over GOP proposal for voter ID requirements
item.description: The article discusses a recent development in Georgia politics involving a proposed voter ID requirement that has sparked immediate backlash from students. The headline references a 'modern-day poll tax' scheme by the GOP, suggesting that the policy would create barriers to voting similar to historical poll taxes that disproportionately affected minority voters. The article mentions a rally held at the Cobb County Convention Center in Atlanta, Georgia, where attendees held flags in support of US Senator Jon Ossoff and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms. The rally appears to be part of a broader political effort to oppose the proposed voter ID requirements. The article notes that the backlash from students is swift and significant, with students expressing concerns that the policy would make voting more difficult for many citizens, particularly those from marginalized communities. item.title: Supreme Court Rejects DOJ Bid to Set Aside 20,000 California Mail-In Ballots
item.description:
The U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Justice Department's emergency request to require California to set aside approximately 20,000 mail-in ballots ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, delivering a legal setback to President Donald Trump's administration. The department had sought to segregate ballots cast by voters it suspected of being noncitizens, relying on a database that officials acknowledged contained significant errors.
The justices denied the request on Monday without recording any dissents or requesting opposition briefs, prompting criticism and celebration among Democratic lawmakers, election attorneys, and political commentators who viewed the decision as a victory for voting rights and the integrity of the electoral process.

item.title: Vintage Photographs Document American Barbershops in the 1940s
item.description:
A collection of vintage photographs offers a glimpse into the traditional barbershops of the 1940s, documenting their interiors, equipment, and role in everyday social life. The images capture an era when barbershops were important neighborhood establishments, serving not only as places for haircuts and shaves but also as gathering spaces where men could meet, talk, and exchange news.
The photographs showcase characteristic features of mid-20th-century barbershops, including polished chrome barber chairs, large mirrors, traditional barber poles, and practical workspaces designed for grooming services. These details provide a visual record of the equipment, furnishings, and atmosphere associated with the profession during the decade.

item.title: Namibian Afrobeat Singer Nally Simson Dies in Crash That Kills Seven
item.description:
Namibian Afrobeat singer Nally Simson, known professionally as Nally, has died at the age of 33 in a head-on collision that killed seven people on Sunday morning, November 1, 2026. The accident occurred at approximately 4:00 a.m. at the Elim Curve along the Okahao-Oshakati main road in Namibia's Omusati region.
According to Omusati regional police commander Commissioner Ismael Basson, the crash involved a bakkie and an SUV. Six occupants of one vehicle and the SUV's driver died at the scene. Authorities confirmed that all seven victims lost their lives in the collision.
Nally's brother, Benjamin Simson, publicly confirmed the musician's death. He also appealed to the public and members of the media to respect the family's privacy and allow them time to mourn without unwanted interference.

item.title: Josh Hartnett, Emma Thompson and Other Actors Join Rebecca Miller’s Margaret Wise Brown Biopic
item.description:
Rebecca Miller’s upcoming biographical film, Moonsong: A Life In Seven Verses, has expanded its cast with several prominent actors, including Josh Hartnett, Emma Thompson, Sally Hawkins, Danny Huston, Robert Aramayo and Chloe Pirrie. They will join previously announced stars Elle Fanning and Julianne Moore in the project, which is scheduled to begin filming in May 2027.
Fanning will portray Margaret Wise Brown, the celebrated American children's author behind classics such as Goodnight Moon and The Runaway Bunny. Moore will play poet Michael Strange, while Hartnett will portray socialite William “Big Bill” Gaston. The film is set in 1930s New York and explores Brown's development as a writer, her unconventional approach to children's literature and her relationships with artists and educators.

item.description:
In an opinion article, John Casey argues that the Republican Party's 2026 midterm campaign has become increasingly chaotic, using a photograph of Donald Trump's windblown comb-over as a metaphor for what he describes as the party's political disarray. He contends that Republicans are struggling to maintain public confidence amid Trump's low approval ratings and widespread voter frustration over the rising costs of groceries, gasoline, health care, and housing.
The columnist highlights several examples of Republican candidates offering economic responses that he considers disconnected from voters' everyday concerns. Mississippi Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith faced criticism after suggesting that consumers struggling with high beef prices could choose other protein sources. item.title: Haley Stevens faces criticism after endorsing Republican candidate on conservative media platform
item.description: US Representative Haley Stevens, a Michigan Democrat who lost the Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, faced criticism from media and political observers after endorsing Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on a conservative media platform. The incident occurred following her attendance at Perfecting Church in Detroit, Michigan, on November 1, 2026. Stevens defended her decision to endorse Rogers during a segment on a MAGA-affiliated show, where she made a comment about 'next stop Mar-a-Lago,' referencing Donald Trump's Florida estate. The remark drew immediate mockery from critics who questioned her political alignment and the strategic implications of her endorsement. item.title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration's Bid to Set Aside 20,000 California Ballots
item.description:
The U.S. Supreme Court rejected a last-minute appeal from the Trump administration on Monday night seeking to require California to set aside approximately 20,000 ballots cast by voters suspected of being ineligible to vote. The decision marked a setback for the administration's efforts to challenge the handling of ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
Earlier Monday, the Department of Justice had asked the Supreme Court to intervene and order California election officials to segregate the disputed ballots. The administration's request followed concerns about the eligibility of voters included on a list compiled by federal authorities.
However, the DOJ had previously acknowledged in lower court proceedings that the dataset used to identify the voters contained numerous errors. Those inaccuracies raised questions about the reliability of the list and the justification for withholding ballots from being counted.

item.title: Former Prosecutor Says DOJ Has Failed to Alter 2026 Midterm Election Rules
item.description:
The Trump administration's efforts to use the courts to influence the administration of the 2026 midterm elections have largely failed, according to Harry Litman, a former federal prosecutor and legal commentator. In a recent essay published on his Substack newsletter, Talking Feds, Litman argued that the Department of Justice (DOJ) has been unable to secure major changes to election procedures despite a series of legal challenges and enforcement actions.
Litman cited 31 unsuccessful attempts by the Justice Department to obtain state voter registration records, its effort to gain control over California's election administration, and several unsuccessful attempts to prosecute individuals accused of illegally voting. He also described the department's changing demands concerning voter registration lists, including an initial list of approximately 190,000 people that was subsequently reduced to around 20,000, as well as attempts to obtain rapid judicial action.

item.title: Walking Speed Linked to Lower Mortality Risk in Long-Term Study
item.description: A study published in JAMA Network Open followed 4,067 U.K. adults with an average age of 69 over nearly 12 years to examine the relationship between walking speed and mortality risk. Participants completed a walking test at their normal pace and wore wrist activity trackers for nine days to measure everyday walking speed. Researchers found that faster walking speed in both settings was associated with a lower risk of death, even after accounting for other health and lifestyle factors. During the study period, 739 participants died. item.title: How Radiation Creates the Blue Color in Topaz Birthstones
item.description: The article explains that November's birthstone, topaz, often appears in a brilliant blue color in jewelry stores, but this blue is not natural. Instead, the stone is treated with radiation to alter its crystal structure, creating color centers that absorb specific wavelengths of light. The process involves ionizing radiation, which knocks electrons out of their normal states, leaving electron vacancies or 'holes.' These trapped electrons and holes form color centers that change the stone's appearance. The article clarifies that while radiation is used in the treatment, the resulting blue topaz is not radioactive. Neutron irradiation in a nuclear reactor can temporarily make the stone radioactive, but it is held until radioactivity decays to safe levels before sale. The mineral topaz, with the chemical formula Al₂SiO₄(F,OH)₂, contains fluorine but is not dangerous like hydrofluoric acid. item.title: Bfloat16 Rounding Issues Cause Near-Complete Stagnation in RL Policy Updates
item.description: The article discusses a critical issue in reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for language models, where standard bfloat16 (bf16) rounding discards over 99% of parameter updates. Modern frameworks like Verl, TRL, and OpenRLHF maintain master weights in fp32 within PyTorch but serve rollouts using a bf16 copy in inference engines such as vLLM or SGLang. The conversion from fp32 to bf16 uses round-to-nearest, which creates a 'dead zone' where small updates are rounded to zero. At typical RL learning rates (1e-6 to 3e-7), nearly all per-parameter updates fall below the threshold, causing the inference engine to serve a model that is effectively frozen. The Stanford paper by Andrew Gao and William Gao demonstrates that only 0.4-0.5% of weights change per optimizer step, with weights needing 50-200 steps to cross a bf16 grid boundary. This discrepancy leads to a significant mismatch between the trained model and the one used for rollouts, as evidenced by lower scores on checkpoints co

Arizona state representatives John Gillette and Rachel Keshel, alongside Turning Point Action's Tyler Bowyer, have circulated allegations on social media, suggesting that a significant number of Republican ballots were not delivered, with Bowyer claiming over 10% of Republicans in some precincts reported no ballot arrival. However, Pima County Recorder Gabriella Cázares-Kelly, who oversees voter registration and early voting, has dismissed these claims as baseless. She stated that the county's office investigated and confirmed that 480,000 ballots were sent out on October 7, with 97% delivered by the USPS, and the remaining 3% were undeliverable due to issues like P.O. boxes or rural addresses. item.title: Nobel Laureate Calls for Nationalizing Starlink Amid Ukraine Internet Access Concerns
item.description: The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk personally ordered a slowdown of internet access to Ukraine, prompting Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman to call for the U.S. to nationalize Musk's Starlink/Starshield satellite network. Krugman's proposal, echoed by David Frum and Matt Stoller, argues that Starlink, heavily subsidized by U.S. government contracts and reliant on U.S. infrastructure, should not be subject to Musk's 'personal whims.' Senator Adam Schiff demanded an investigation and Musk's testimony before Congress, citing life-or-death consequences for Ukraine. The article details historical precedents for nationalization in U.S. history, including Woodrow Wilson's World War I railroads and telegraph nationalizations, FDR's WWII manufacturing and mining seizures, and more recent examples like the 2008 financial crisis. item.title: Human Activity Prevents Onset of Next Ice Age, Study Finds
item.description: A new study published in the journal Science suggests that human-driven climate change has halted the onset of the next ice age. Researchers led by Nicolás Young of Columbia University analyzed the Barnes Ice Cap (BIC) in Canada, which is a remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS) that once covered much of North America. The study used two primary methods: measuring cosmogenic beryllium-10 in rocks and analyzing carbon-14 in vegetation to track the ice cap's historical growth and retreat. The findings indicate that the next ice age was poised to begin around 2,000 years ago, as the Earth entered a cooling phase following the Holocene interglacial period. However, the expansion of the ice sheet was interrupted by rising global temperatures, particularly since the 1960s, when anthropogenic warming reversed the ice cap's growth. The researchers note that the Barnes Ice Cap reached its historical maximum around 1960, after which it began to shrink due to increasing summer temperatures. Th

item.title: Reddit Data Extraction Methods for 2026: API, Historical Archives, and Web Scraping
item.description: The article outlines three viable methods for extracting Reddit data in 2026, addressing the changes following Reddit's 2023 API pricing announcement. The first method utilizes Reddit's official API with PRAW (Python Reddit API Wrapper), which remains free for non-commercial use with a rate limit of approximately 60 requests per minute. The second method involves accessing historical data through Arctic Shift, an academic project hosting Reddit data dumps via Academic Torrents, offering archives dating back to 2007. The third method employs web scraping of old.reddit.com, which provides static HTML content without JavaScript, allowing for more straightforward data extraction. The article emphasizes legal considerations, noting that while Reddit's Terms of Service prohibit scraping, the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) does not criminalize scraping publicly available data, as established in the HiQ v. item.description: The author recounts receiving nearly 2,000 political fundraising texts meant for another person, highlighting a systemic issue in campaign data management. Sterling's CEO acknowledged data inaccuracies but defended the practice as necessary for fundraising. item.title: Chancellor Healey shifts focus from 2030 renewable energy target to bill reduction
item.description: Chancellor John Healey has effectively abandoned Labour's manifesto pledge to generate 95% of electricity from renewable sources by 2030, according to The Telegraph. In his maiden Budget, Healey instructed the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) to prioritize funding for green energy projects that lower consumer bills and can be easily integrated into the National Grid. This policy shift makes it significantly harder to approve new offshore wind farms, which were central to Labour's 2024 election promise. The changes address grid connection backlogs and high costs of green levies, but critics argue they undermine Ed Miliband's vision of 'clean power by 2030' as the 'biggest transformation of our energy system in decades.' While Miliband's office denied opposition to the changes, government sources confirmed the 2030 target is now 'effectively dead.' item.description: The Philadelphia Eagles suffered their sixth straight loss in a 27-10 defeat to the Washington Commanders on Sunday Night Football. After building an early 10-0 lead with a 40-yard field goal by Jake Elliott and a three-yard touchdown run by Saquon Barkley following a Washington turnover, the Eagles failed to score again. Washington capitalized on the momentum, with Jayden Daniels throwing for 217 yards and a touchdown, while kicker Drew Stevens contributed three field goals, including a 56-yarder in the first quarter and a 39-yarder before halftime. Daniels then connected with Treylon Burks for a 53-yard gain, leading to a 25-yard field goal by Stevens. item.description: Egypt has entered into a $1 billion financing agreement with the World Bank, aimed at enhancing economic competitiveness, improving the business environment, and supporting the country's green transition. The agreement is part of Egypt's broader strategy to mobilize development financing from international and regional institutions to strengthen economic resilience against external shocks. The funding aligns with the World Bank Group's 2023-2027 Country Partnership Framework for Egypt, which includes a $7 billion financial envelope over five years. item.title: Wolves Enter Villages as Google Clears Forest for AI Data Centers in Finland
item.description: Google has faced significant backlash in Finland after clearing 1,300 acres of forest for AI data centers, leading to wolves and other wildlife roaming into nearby villages. The Finnish Association for Nature Conservation and the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) have condemned Google's actions, citing environmental policy violations. The company's country manager apologized for unauthorized forest clearings near Muhos, which have transformed 816 acres of forest into mud. Google has been ordered to cease work on 500 acres of cleared forest, 55 miles southeast of Otanmäki. Local residents, including Anni Ranta, a lifelong resident of Otanmäki, report wolves entering villages as animals displaced from their natural habitat. The situation has raised concerns about human safety and potential Russian aggression, with Ranta noting Finland could become a target for Russian actions due to the data centers. item.title: Niddy Impekoven: The Expressionist Dancer Who Captured the Spirit of the 1920s and 1930s
item.description: Luise 'Niddy' Impekoven (November 2, 1904 – November 20, 2002) was a German dancer who rose to international fame during the 1920s and 1930s as a leading figure in the modern German dance movement known as Ausdruckstanz. Starting as a child prodigy in the Weimar era, she transitioned into a celebrated expressionist dance superstar before retiring abruptly in 1934 at the age of 30. Impekoven's performances were characterized by dramatic, whimsical, and emotive styles, often set to classical music such as Beethoven's 'Moonlight Sonata.' She became particularly famous for her 'doll dances,' which mimicked jerky, puppet-like movements inspired by avant-garde artistic dolls. Her work resonated with elite intellectual circles, attracting admirers like authors Thomas Mann and Arthur Schnitzler. item.title: Sally Field: A Career Spanning Six Decades of Emotional Depth and Range
item.description: Sally Field, born in 1946, has established herself as one of the most authentic and affecting performers in American cinema over more than six decades. She first gained recognition in the 1960s with lighthearted television roles in 'Gidget' and 'The Flying Nun,' before transitioning to more dramatic roles that showcased her emotional depth and resilience. Field's career highlights include winning Academy Awards for Best Actress for her performances in 'Norma Rae' (1979) and 'Places in the Heart' (1984), roles that demonstrated both her strength and vulnerability. She continued to deliver memorable performances in films such as 'Steel Magnolias,' 'Mrs. Doubtfire,' 'Forrest Gump,' and 'Lincoln.' Throughout her career, Field has maintained a reputation for emotional honesty and remarkable range, making her a standout figure in American film. item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that President Donald Trump has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of Javits Frimpong, a 15-year-old Ghanaian immigrant who was fatally shot in the Bronx last week. The teen was heading to school on Thursday morning when he was shot in the abdomen and later pronounced dead at a hospital. No arrests have been made in connection with the shooting, which remains under investigation. Mayor Mamdani stated on X that the president had agreed to grant the visa immediately, allowing the mother, Doris Adu Gyamfi, to travel from Ghana to attend her son's funeral. "The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," Mamdani wrote. "Javits Frimpong's mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person." item.description: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk is navigating a deepening constitutional crisis in Poland following a televised address where he emphasized the need to restore the rule of law after years of interference by the Law and Justice (PiS) party in the judiciary. The dispute centers on the composition of Poland's Constitutional Tribunal, with tensions escalating as President Karol Nawrocki attempted to enter the Tribunal building amid a deadlock over new judge appointments. Tusk's government claims it is implementing reforms to align with European court rulings and the Venice Commission's recommendations, while PiS accuses the government of attempting a coup. item.title: China's clean tech exports set new records, reducing global emissions by 8.4 billion tonnes
item.description: China's clean technology exports have reached unprecedented levels, with significant implications for global carbon emissions. According to a report by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), China's clean tech exports in 2026 could prevent approximately 8,400 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions over the lifetime of the equipment. This represents about 24% of annual global emissions, surpassing the combined emissions of the United States and India. The report highlights a 61% increase in electric vehicle exports, a 45% jump in wind turbine shipments, a 39% surge in battery exports, and a 22% growth in solar equipment exports during the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. Southeast Asia emerged as a major destination, with clean energy exports to the region jumping nearly 160% year-on-year. Experts warn that AI chatbots can 'hallucinate' misinformation, presenting it as credible, and lead to 'cognitive surrender' where users stop thinking critically. item.description: Following the deadly December 14 attack at Bondi Beach during a Hanukkah celebration, which left 15 people dead including a 10-year-old girl, New South Wales police have initiated a new security measure involving armed patrols in high-traffic areas. The Armed Response Command (ARC) will deploy specially trained officers equipped with long-arm rifles in tourist hotspots like Luna Park and near places of worship, aiming to prevent, deter, and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active shooter incidents. The operation, which will eventually include 250 officers, has drawn mixed reactions from residents: some find the visible presence of armed officers unnerving, while others feel it enhances their sense of safety. item.description: Stack Overflow, the long-standing programming question-and-answer platform, is experiencing a significant decline in monthly question volume, with data from the Stack Exchange API confirming fewer than 1,000 questions created in September 2026. The author of the post, Frank Chu, verified this by directly querying the API rather than relying on charts or secondary sources. His analysis shows September 2026 had 969 questions, down from 5,263 in October 2025 and 23,162 in October 2024, representing a 95.8% decline over two years. The trend indicates a 99.3% drop from October 2020 levels, when the site processed over 140,000 questions monthly. Chu's methodology involved using the Stack Exchange API's /questions endpoint with specific date ranges, ensuring accurate counts of questions created within each month. item.title: Rocky Linux Founder Develops AI-Assisted Kernel That Mimics Linux Compatibility
item.description: Gregory Kurtzer, the creator of Rocky Linux and former CentOS developer, has developed a new operating system kernel called Ginux in just 11 days with the assistance of AI. Unlike traditional Linux distributions, Ginux is not a fork of the Linux kernel but a completely independent, Rust-first x86-64 kernel. It features its own memory management, scheduler, process model, filesystems, networking, and device support, all written from scratch. The key innovation is that Ginux implements the Linux ABI (Application Binary Interface), allowing existing Linux binaries to run unmodified on the new system. This means users can run standard Linux applications without needing to recompile them, making it a direct compatibility layer rather than a replacement kernel. Currently, Ginux is only functional within a QEMU virtual machine, lacking support for physical hardware, GPUs, NVMe storage, and undergoing independent security audits. item.title: Indiana Reports 31 Measles Cases in Three-Day Surge
item.description: The Indiana Department of Health has reported a significant increase in measles cases across the state, with 31 new cases identified within a three-day period. This brings the total number of cases for the year to 97 as of Friday's update. LaGrange County remains the most affected area, reporting 22 cases this year, up from 10 cases reported just three days prior. Elkhart County has also seen a rise, with two new cases bringing their total to three. Health officials emphasize that most of the cases involve individuals who are not vaccinated, highlighting the importance of maintaining up-to-date immunization records. Medical experts are urging the public to ensure they and their families are fully vaccinated against measles, which can lead to severe complications if left unchecked. item.description: Armed police in the UK have conducted their first-ever training exercise simulating an attack on a shipment of radioactive material being transported from the Dounreay nuclear site. The Civil Nuclear Constabulary (CNC) collaborated with Police Scotland and emergency services to stage a scenario where armed attackers deliberately crashed a vehicle to block a lorry carrying radioactive material near Georgemas Junction, a railway station approximately six miles from Dounreay on Scotland's north Caithness coast. The exercise, held late last month, involved an employee at Dounreay being 'arrested' as part of the simulated attack. The CNC emphasized that this was a scenario never before tested, requiring significant preparation and coordination across multiple agencies. item.description: The article discusses the strategic use of Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 model in AI engineering contexts. It emphasizes that developers shouldn't automatically default to the most capable model for every task, but rather should start with the smallest model that meets a verifiable quality threshold. The recommended approach is to establish a policy where Haiku 5.5 is used as the default for bounded, easily verifiable tasks, with exceptions routed to stronger models or human operators. item.description: The FBI has identified North Korean hackers as responsible for the largest cryptocurrency heist in history, which resulted in the theft of over $6 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. According to the FBI's statement, the attack was carried out by a group known as TraderTraitor, which was also linked to a previous $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange in 2023. The hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currencies within minutes, leaving Binance to cover 90% of the missing assets with its own reserves. The FBI has urged crypto exchanges and blockchain analytics companies to block transactions associated with specific addresses to prevent the laundering of stolen funds. item.title: Byoky: Open-source wallet for AI API keys
item.description: Byoky is an open-source wallet designed to securely manage AI API keys, available as a Chrome and Firefox extension and as mobile apps for iOS and Android. The wallet allows users to store their API keys for various providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Gemini, encrypted directly on their devices. Instead of pasting keys into application settings, which compromises control, Byoky follows a model similar to MetaMask, where apps request access to the keys, and users approve or revoke permissions with a single click. The system uses AES-256-GCM encryption with a password-derived key through 600,000 PBKDF2 iterations, requiring a minimum 12-character password for security. Developers can integrate Byoky into their applications using its SDK, which supports streaming, tool calls, and image inputs. item.title: Alaska Voters Weigh Repealing Ranked-Choice Voting System
item.description: Alaskans are once again considering the repeal of their ranked-choice voting system, which was approved by voters in 2020 and narrowly avoided being overturned in 2024. The current debate centers on whether to eliminate the system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. Proponents, including state Republican leaders and President Trump, argue that the system confuses voters. Opponents counter that repealing it would diminish voter power. Under the ranked-choice system, Alaskans participate in an open primary where candidates from all parties compete on a single ballot. The top four candidates advance to the general election, where voters rank their preferences. If no candidate secures a majority, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated, and their votes are redistributed according to voters' second choices. item.title: Jean d'Ylen: A Pioneer of Bold and Colorful French Poster Art in the 1920s
item.description: Jean d'Ylen, born Jean Paul Béguin in Paris in 1886, was a prominent French poster artist known for his vibrant, imaginative, and highly colorful designs. After studying at the Bernard Palissy School of Fine Arts, he transitioned to poster art following World War I, joining the renowned Vercasson printing house where he succeeded Leonetto Cappiello as a principal artist. Over his career, d'Ylen created over 200 posters advertising a wide range of products, from wines and spirits to tires and cigarettes. His work is characterized by vivid colors, dynamic compositions, and whimsical, larger-than-life characters that captured attention immediately. Despite his career being cut short by his death in 1938 at the age of 52, d'Ylen remains one of the most inventive and vibrant poster artists of the interwar period. item.title: Chinese Space Agency Details Plans for Lunar Base Using Pressurized Rovers After First Crewed Landing
item.description: The Chinese Manned Space Agency (CMSA) has confirmed its plans for a crewed lunar landing and subsequent base construction during the 7th Manned Space Program Symposium held in China on October 31 and November 1. The program requires two launches of the Long March 10 rocket: one to send the Lanyue lunar module to the Moon, followed by another to deliver the Mengzhou-Y spacecraft carrying three astronauts. The Mengzhou-Y will dock with the Lanyue in lunar orbit, with two astronauts transferring to the lunar module while one remains in orbit. item.title: Laura La Plante: The Silent Film Star Who Defined 1920s Hollywood
item.description: Laura La Plante (November 1, 1904 – October 14, 1996) was an American film actress who rose to prominence during the silent film era. Known for her bright dimples, easygoing charm, and signature bleached-blonde bobbed hair, La Plante became Universal Pictures' most popular star and highest-grossing box-office attraction in the 1920s, appearing in over 60 films during the decade. Her career began as a teenage extra to support her family, with early roles in shorts based on the Bringing Up Father comic strip (1920) and the acclaimed silent film The Old Swimmin' Hole (1921). She built her reputation co-starring in a half-dozen Hoot Gibson Westerns before being named a WAMPAS Baby Star in 1923, which led Universal to grant her more substantial dramatic and comedic leads. For her role in the 1924 film Butterfly, she adopted a fashionable short bob and blonde dye, a quintessential 'flapper' style that became her trademark. item.description: The article details a technical quirk in the curl command-line tool that made it accidentally Turing-complete for a period of nine months, from version 8.12 through 8.16. A proof-of-concept demonstrating the addition of 2 + 3 was provided, along with instructions for building a local curl 8.12.0 binary to test the behavior. item.title: NASA Swift Observatory to Reenter Earth's Atmosphere Following Failed Rescue Attempt
item.description: The Swift Observatory, a NASA telescope launched in 2004 to study gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic phenomena, is on the verge of reentering Earth's atmosphere after a failed rescue mission. The U.S. Space Force predicts the 1.5-ton telescope will crash on or around Friday, with most of it burning up during reentry. However, some denser components made of tungsten and mirror parts may survive and potentially land in oceanic areas or over regions including Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, Central and South America. The telescope, which has operated for 22 years, was designed to rapidly respond to cosmic events, earning its name from its swift maneuverability. Its mission included discovering over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 supernovae, as well as observing comets, asteroids, and black holes. item.title: New research challenges comet theory as source of life's building blocks on Earth
item.description: A new study published in Scientific Reports challenges a decades-old theory that comets delivered the organic molecules necessary for life to Earth. The research, led by Richard Anslow of the University of Cambridge, used computer simulations to analyze comet impacts during Earth's early history. The findings suggest that the high-speed impacts would have destroyed fragile organic molecules rather than delivering them intact. The study simulated 100,000 comet impacts over 4 billion years ago, finding that 54% of simulations showed no impact at all, while only a 'tiny minority' of impacts (46%) had one to three collisions. Crucially, even successful impacts would have needed to occur in a 'perfect location' with existing conditions like liquid water and other chemicals, making the process unlikely. item.title: Buzludja Monument: Bulgaria's Abandoned Communist-Era Concrete UFO
item.description: The article details a visit to the Buzludja Monument in Bulgaria, a massive concrete structure built during the communist era that has since been abandoned. Constructed between 1971 and 1981, the monument was intended to honor the first assembly of Bulgarian socialists held in 1891. The project involved dynamiting the peak of Mount Hadzhi Dimitar, reducing its height by nine meters, and required significant infrastructure development including a new road to the remote site. The construction cost approximately 15 million Bulgarian leva (equivalent to about 40 million euros today), with suspicions of corruption during the communist regime. The monument was inaugurated in 1981 with a 150,000-watt red star, visible from the Danube to the Aegean Sea. However, following the fall of communism in Bulgaria on November 9, 1989, the structure was abandoned, leading to deterioration from weather, vandalism, and neglect. item.description: The article presents a collection of 40 Photochrom photographs from the late 19th century, offering a vivid and historically significant glimpse into life in the Netherlands during that era. Photochrom was a technique that applied realistic color to black-and-white photographs using multiple lithographic stones, creating images with remarkable clarity and warmth. The photographs showcase various locations across the Netherlands, including Amsterdam's iconic landmarks such as Dam Square, the Nieuwe Kerk, and the Rijksmuseum, as well as Haarlem's city hall and windmills, and rural scenes from Marken Island. Each image captures the architecture, traditional costumes, and daily activities of the period, preserving the atmosphere of the Netherlands more than 120 years ago. item.description: NASA has issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking proposals from commercial companies to reboost, service, or safely dispose of the Hubble Space Telescope. item.title: Boston Researchers Identify Distinct Tumor Characteristics in Younger Colorectal Cancer Patients
item.description: Boston researchers have identified significant differences in tumor cells between younger and older colorectal cancer patients, potentially paving the way for more targeted treatments. The study, led by researchers from Mass General Brigham, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, and the Broad Institute, analyzed 189 tumors and over 850,000 individual cell nuclei from more than 50 patients under age 50. Dr. Ana Anderson, a senior co-author, explained that younger patients' tumors contained a higher proportion of stromal cells—connective tissue cells that can suppress the immune system and create barriers preventing drug penetration. These findings may explain why colorectal cancer is increasingly diagnosed in younger adults, with rates rising nearly 3% annually among those under 50. The American Cancer Society reports colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of cancer-related death in this age group. item.title: A browser-based project seeks new periodic orbits in the three-body problem
item.description: The article describes a computational project that uses browser-based technology to search for new periodic orbits in the three-body problem. The project involves tracing the motion of three masses under Newtonian gravity, testing various initial conditions to find paths that nearly return to their starting points. The system checks these paths at high precision, using a 'bounded Newton shooting' method to refine initial conditions and periods. A 'promising return' is a proposed orbit that is first checked against known orbits in an atlas before being recorded. The system refines these proposals to 106 bits and confirms them in double precision, with some orbits requiring additional verification at higher bit depths. Only verified periodic results are added to the 'checked loops' database, which is labeled as linearly stable or unstable based on small planar perturbations. item.description: Prescription eye drops such as Vizz and Yuvezzi, approved by the FDA in 2025 and 2026 respectively, aim to treat presbyopia, the age-related condition that makes it difficult to focus on close objects. These drops work by shrinking the pupils, creating a pinhole effect that improves near vision. The drops can help users read smaller text without enlarging the font, potentially improving near vision from 20/60 to 20/30, but results vary based on individual vision, print size, and lighting conditions. Side effects include reduced night vision, headaches, and potential risks like retinal tears, which necessitate a pre-treatment eye exam. Cost is also a factor, with Vizz priced at $79 for 25 doses and Yuvezzi at $79 for 30 days. Health officials report a nearly 50% lethality rate, with 2,788 recoveries. item.description: The Mercedes-Benz T80, a six-wheeled land speed record vehicle developed in 1939, was designed to achieve speeds exceeding 600 km/h (373 mph) but never completed an official run due to the outbreak of World War II. Conceived by racing driver Hans Stuck and engineered by Dr. Ferdinand Porsche under the sponsorship of Daimler-Benz, the project aimed to showcase German technological prowess under Adolf Hitler's regime. The vehicle's design included innovative features such as a hydraulic torque converter, mechanical anti-spin control, and a special fuel mixture to prevent engine detonation. item.title: Pingualuit Crater: A Natural Wonder with the Purest Water on Earth
item.description: The Pingualuit Crater, located in the remote Arctic region of Quebec, Canada, is renowned for containing the purest water found in nature. Discovered in 1943 by a U.S. military reconnaissance flight, the crater is a nearly perfect circle measuring three kilometers in diameter, filled with water that has no external sources of inflow or outflow. The lake's purity stems from its unique hydrological system: water enters only through precipitation and leaves solely through evaporation, resulting in extremely low salinity levels—hundreds of times lower than those found in rivers or the Great Lakes. This makes Pingualuit one of the most transparent lakes on the planet. The crater, formed approximately 1.5 million years ago by an asteroid impact, is one of the best-preserved impact craters on Earth, with minimal erosion due to successive glaciations. The Panthers' quarterback Bryce Young completed 23-of-41 passes for 209 yards with a touchdown and an interception, but was sacked six times, including four by rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton.

item.title: Crocodiles' Climate Preference Explains Survival After Dinosaur-Killing Asteroid Impact
item.description: Scientists from University College London have uncovered a key factor in why crocodiles survived the asteroid impact that wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. Their research, published in Science Advances, reveals that crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic event. The study analyzed over 7,000 fossils and climate data from 400 species spanning 245 million years. Researchers found that while dinosaurs' habitats contracted severely following the impact, crocodile relatives maintained access to suitable tropical regions near the equator. These areas provided critical refuges where populations could persist and eventually recover. The study also highlights that crocodiles' evolutionary history shows remarkable consistency in their climate preferences, despite their diverse body forms and lifestyles. item.title: American Photographer Captures Bunker Interior After Berlin Fall in 1945
item.description: In the final days of April 1945, as Soviet forces advanced into Berlin, Adolf Hitler and Eva Braun died by suicide in the Führerbunker, a reinforced concrete shelter beneath the Reich Chancellery. American photographer William Vandivert, working for LIFE magazine, entered the captured complex shortly after the Soviet victory and documented its interior, abandoned belongings, and the wreckage of the Chancellery above. His photographs, taken in the immediate aftermath of Berlin's fall, provide a rare visual record of the Third Reich's final days. Vandivert's images, published in LIFE in July 1945, captured the bunker's offices, private quarters, and scattered papers, including news reports dated April 29, the day before Hitler and Braun's deaths. The Führerbunker, constructed in stages with the main structure completed in October 1944, was a heavily fortified underground complex measuring 27 meters long and 22 meters wide, with walls 3.5 meters thick. item.description: NASA astronauts Anil Menon and Joshua Kutryk successfully completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station's port-side truss structure. This installation marks a significant step in the ongoing power upgrade of the International Space Station, which will increase the station's available power by up to 30% once all eight arrays are installed. The astronauts installed the array on the 2A electrical power channel, bringing the total number of arrays to seven. The final spacewalk scheduled for November 5 will install the eighth and final array on the 3B power channel, completing the solar power expansion. The completed mission, designated U.S. spacewalk 100, marked Menon's fourth spacewalk and Kutryk's first, and was the 285th spacewalk conducted to support the International Space Station. item.description: European countries are increasingly utilizing waste heat from crematoria to warm homes and public facilities, marking a growing trend in sustainable funeral practices. The practice, which began in Redditch, England, in 2011, has since expanded across Europe, with projects in Aberdeen, Scotland, and Kangasala, Finland, demonstrating the feasibility of capturing heat from cremation processes. In Redditch, a heat exchanger captures thermal energy from flue gases emitted during cremation, redirecting it through underground pipes to warm a local swimming pool. This system, operational since 2013, has saved the council tens of thousands of pounds annually in fuel costs. Similar initiatives are emerging elsewhere: Aberdeen's new school will receive waste heat from its crematorium, while Kangasala's upcoming all-electric crematorium will connect to the town's district heating network, supplying over 6,500 homes. The study examined Huayu Wan, a formulation containing 15 ingredients derived from two traditional remedies, Taohong Siwu and Didang decoctions. item.title: OpenAI CEO Argues Against Local AI Computing, Advocates for Centralized Datacenter Use
item.description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has made a controversial statement regarding the allocation of DRAM (Dynamic Random-Access Memory), arguing that it is 'terrible' for the world's limited supply to be distributed among everyday consumers rather than concentrated in datacenters. Altman, speaking in an interview with Cheeky Pint, explained that the current memory crisis, driven by AI datacenter demand, has led to skyrocketing prices and shortages for consumer electronics. He believes that the desire for local AI computing—where individuals run models on their own devices—is misguided, as it leads to inefficient use of scarce resources. 'From a global allocation perspective, it's quite terrible to have everyone have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer. And be used 5% of the time,' Altman stated. He emphasized that centralized cloud computing would maximize utilization of limited hardware resources, which is critical given the constraints on silicon production.

item.title: Antarctic Ocean Currents Reverse Abruptly, Threatening Global Climate Systems
item.description: An international study published in Nature Climate Change reveals a significant shift in Antarctic ocean currents, with the Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) experiencing a rapid reversal in salinity, density, and depth since 2016. The research, led by the University of Melbourne and the Indian Institute of Science, found that declining Antarctic sea ice has abruptly reduced seasonal meltwater delivery, causing the AAIW layer to become warmer, saltier, denser, and deeper within less than a decade. For two decades prior to 2016, the AAIW was replenished with freshwater from seasonal Antarctic sea ice melt, with annual meltwater volumes equivalent to three times the Amazon River's flow. However, after 2016, sea ice decline led to a one-third reduction in freshwater input, triggering rapid salinification and densification. item.title: Patrick Stewart's Death Linked to Alzheimer's and Lewy Body Dementia, Expert Explains
item.description: British actor Patrick Stewart, known for his iconic roles in 'Star Trek: The Next Generation' and the 'X-Men' franchise, died at age 86 on Wednesday, October 29, 2026. His spokesperson confirmed that he passed away from Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, conditions that often co-occur. UCLA neurology professor Dr. Keith Vossel explained that when these two conditions are present together, the individual's decline may be faster compared to having just one of the conditions. Lewy body dementia is the second-most-common form of degenerative dementia, following Alzheimer's disease, and occurs when a protein called alpha-synuclein aggregates in clumps inside the brain. The condition is frequently under-recognized and under-diagnosed because its symptoms overlap with those of Alzheimer's. item.title: Cold Temperatures Activate Muscle-Driven Pathway to Boost Longevity, Study Reveals
item.description: A groundbreaking study published in Nature has uncovered a molecular mechanism by which cold temperatures extend lifespan. Researchers from the University of Cologne identified that mild cold exposure triggers muscle cells to produce dihydrobiopterin (BH2), a metabolite that travels throughout the body to maintain protein homeostasis and support tissue health during aging. The study, conducted on nematode worms (C. elegans) and human cells, reveals that cold temperatures increase production of an enzyme called CAT-4 in muscles, which stimulates BH2 synthesis. This metabolite is then converted into tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), enabling an enzyme to produce tyrosine, an amino acid critical for cellular function. item.description: According to The New York Times, President Donald Trump privately 'erupted' in anger after learning that Alina Habba, a former personal attorney, had secured a lucrative contract with a Venezuelan billionaire family worth over $50 million. The deal, which includes $10 million annually plus bonuses for a four-year term, was reportedly discussed by Trump with aides and allies, who stated he was 'angered' by the amount Habba would earn. Trump reportedly urged Habba to donate part of the funds to his presidential library or another entity bearing his name, and even suggested the Venezuelan family halt further payments. Habba, who previously represented Trump personally and served as U.S. attorney in New Jersey, agreed to become general counsel for Concord Partners, a company linked to the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, in January 2026. item.title: Trump Cancels In-Person Rallies, Shifts to Tele-Rallies Amid Midterm Concerns
item.description: President Donald Trump has faced criticism for canceling in-person campaign rallies and replacing them with tele-rallies during the midterm election season. According to CBS News White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, Trump canceled a Sunday rally in Dubuque, Iowa, and a Saturday event in Salina, Kansas, both of which were intended to bolster support for Republican candidates. The Republican National Committee confirmed these events would now be conducted virtually. Former Obama White House communications director Dan Pfeiffer questioned whether Trump was 'quiet quitting' the midterms, while political analyst Adam Carlson suggested the move reflected panic as Republican support reportedly 'hemorrhages' among undecided voters. Carlson described the strategy as a 'spray-and-pray approach,' noting that tele-rallies featuring Trump lack the energy of in-person events.
